answer:
**Missingness describes a data-collection process, not just an empty cell.** MCAR means missingness is independent of observed and unobserved values under the formulation. MAR allows missingness to depend on observed information. MNAR means dependence on unobserved/missing values remains after conditioning on what is observed. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

**Three examples.** Random sensor packet loss can approximate MCAR. A lab test ordered more often for older patients may be MAR conditional on recorded age and relevant variables. People with very high income declining to report it can be MNAR when that income itself influences nonresponse beyond observed covariates. These are modeling assumptions, not labels that can always be proven from the incomplete data alone.

An `is_missing` feature can be predictive because the decision to measure carries information: a clinician ordering a test may indicate concern, or a user skipping a form field may reflect behavior. That signal can be stronger than a crude imputed value.

**But the signal may not be stable or appropriate.** If the collection policy changes, the model's learned missingness relationship can fail. A proxy for operational practice can also create undesirable feedback or unfairness depending on the use case.

Choose imputation and indicators based on the mechanism and prediction-time availability. Fit imputers inside training folds, evaluate missingness-pattern shifts, and distinguish predicting well under the observed process from recovering the true distribution of missing values.

**Technical details and references.**

MCAR means missingness is independent of observed and missing values. MAR allows dependence on observed variables, after conditioning on which missingness does not depend on the unobserved value. MNAR retains dependence on the missing value itself. These are assumptions about the missingness mechanism, not labels identifiable from the observed table alone. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

A missingness indicator can be highly predictive when measurement is a decision—for example, a specialist orders a test only for concerning cases. That signal may fail if workflow changes and can leak post-outcome actions. Imputation plus an indicator can help prediction but does not solve MNAR identification. Examine collection timing, subgroup missingness, and sensitivity to plausible unobserved values before interpreting effects.
